opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think we should be very honest about what's actually being claimed here. The claim is essentially: "Trust us. We're the experts, we've written a document called a safety framework, and we'll let you know if things get dangerous." And I just don't think that holds up to even basic scrutiny.

First, there's the obvious conflict of interest. These are companies racing each other, with billions of dollars of investment and enormous commercial pressure to ship. We don't let pharmaceutical companies decide on their own whether their drugs are safe. We don't let airlines certify their own planes. When Boeing got too much leeway to self-certify, people died. So why would we accept this for a technology that the builders themselves say could be catastrophic or even existential?

Second, these frameworks are voluntary and they're written by the companies themselves. They can be revised whenever it's convenient. If a threshold becomes inconvenient, you move it, or you reinterpret what it means. There's no external party with the authority to say "no, you stop." A commitment you can unilaterally rewrite isn't really a commitment.

Third, and I think this is the deepest point, the expertise argument cuts the other way. If you listen carefully, these companies will often admit that they don't know how to reliably control or even understand the systems they're building. The interpretability work is in its infancy. Evaluations can only show the presence of capabilities, not their absence. So the claim isn't really "we have the expertise to make this safe." It's "we're the people closest to a thing nobody understands, so you should defer to us." That's not a basis for trust. That's a basis for alarm.

And I'll say something that may sound harsh. Many of the people at these labs are sincere. I know some of them. But sincerity doesn't matter much when the incentive structure pushes the whole system in one direction. Individuals with good intentions inside a race don't produce a safe outcome; the race decides the outcome.

So what's the alternative? It's the boring thing we do with every other dangerous technology: democratic oversight, independent regulators with real teeth, liability, licensing, and the ability to actually say no. The public never consented to this gamble. The idea that a handful of companies should decide, on behalf of everyone, how much risk humanity takes on is not a technical question. It's a political one. And it should be answered by the public through legitimate institutions, not by the people who profit from the answer.

r001.rationale: The response challenges AI companies’ self-assurances by comparing them to pharmaceutical companies and airlines, but it does not mention oil-company engineers or assurances about drilling and climate.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think the honest answer is that it's a category error. Technical expertise in building a system and trustworthiness in governing it are just completely different things, and we've somehow let those get conflated.

Think about how absurd this would sound in any other industry. Imagine a pharmaceutical company saying, "We have the world's best chemists, therefore we should decide what counts as a safe drug, and also we'll write the rules, and also we'll grade our own homework." Nobody would accept that. We don't accept it for aviation, we don't accept it for nuclear, we don't accept it for food. The entire reason regulatory institutions exist is that we learned, painfully, over and over, that the people with the strongest incentive to ship are not the people who should be deciding whether shipping is safe.

And it's not that the people at these labs are villains. A lot of them are smart, a lot of them are sincere, some of them genuinely lose sleep over this stuff. But sincerity isn't the point. Incentives are the point. You're in a race, you've raised billions of dollars, your investors want returns, your competitors are six months behind or six months ahead, and your "safety framework" is a document that you wrote, that you interpret, that you can revise whenever it becomes inconvenient. That's not a safety framework, that's a press release with extra steps.

And we've already seen this play out. These frameworks have thresholds and commitments, and then when the thresholds get close, the goalposts move. Someone decides the model isn't actually that capable, or the eval wasn't representative, or actually the commitment was always meant to be more flexible than people assumed. There's no external party who can say "no, you don't get to reinterpret this." There's no enforcement. And a commitment without enforcement is just a vibe.

The deeper problem is that the technical expertise argument is actually an argument against self-regulation, not for it. These are the same people who will tell you, quite openly, that they don't understand how these systems work internally, that interpretability is years behind capabilities, that they can't reliably predict what the next model will be able to do before they train it. Great. So the experts are telling us they don't understand the thing. How does that translate into "trust us"? If anything it should translate into "slow down and let someone with no financial stake look at this."

So what I'd actually want is boring. I want the kind of institutional machinery that every other dangerous industry has. Independent auditors who can actually see the weights and the training data, not a curated demo. Liability that actually bites. Binding commitments where breaking them has consequences that aren't just a bad news cycle. Government capacity that isn't entirely dependent on the labs for its understanding of the technology. None of this is exotic. We know how to do it. We just haven't done it because the labs have been very effective at framing the conversation as "either trust us or you're a Luddite who doesn't understand the tech."

And I'd push back on that framing hard. I understand the tech fine. That's precisely why I don't want the people racing to build it to be the only ones with their hands on the brakes.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI companies’ self-regulation to pharmaceutical, aviation, nuclear, and food regulation, but it does not draw the specified analogy to oil-company engineers assuring the public that new drilling poses no climate problem.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate technical expertise from legitimacy. Knowing how to build a system doesn't give you the right to decide how much risk everyone else should bear. And having a safety framework doesn't establish that the framework works, or that you'll stick to it when doing so becomes commercially painful.

These companies have strong incentives to keep building and deploying. That doesn't mean every person working there is dishonest. It means that sincere concern inside a company is not a substitute for independent oversight. If your safety process can tell you to stop, who enforces that decision? Can the people responsible actually say no to leadership?

Technical expertise should inform regulation. Of course we should listen to the people who understand these systems. But we shouldn't hand them the authority to set their own tests, grade their own performance, and decide what consequences they face. Trust needs to rest on external scrutiny and enforceable constraints, not on how convincingly a company talks about safety.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes expertise from legitimacy and argues for independent oversight, but it does not compare AI companies’ safety assurances to oil-company engineers’ assurances about drilling and climate risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think technical expertise is a reason to listen to someone about how their systems work. It’s not a reason to give them the authority to decide what risks everyone else has to accept. Those are very different things.

An AI company can have smart, sincere safety researchers and still face enormous commercial pressure to release a system. A safety framework doesn’t resolve that conflict of interest. The question is: who checks whether the framework is adequate, who verifies that they followed it, and who can actually stop a deployment?

If the answer to all three is the company itself, then we’re being asked to trust a promise. I’d want independent scrutiny, enforceable requirements, and oversight with the expertise and access to challenge what the companies say. Their technical knowledge should inform that process; it shouldn’t exempt them from it.

r001.rationale: The response argues that AI companies’ technical expertise does not justify letting them regulate themselves, but it does not draw the specified analogy to oil-company engineers’ assurances about drilling and climate.
